To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
TCs are activated by spontaneous glutamatergic EPSPs and GABAergic IPSPs and that the TCs are the only retinal cells that receive efferent innervation.

TCs are excited by glutamate from retinal amacrine neurons, and by GABA from other amacrine neurons, that TCs generate action potentials in response to these excitatory synaptic inputs, and that TCs are therefore not merely slaves to descending midbrain input.

efferent target cells in the avium retina receive glutamatergic input from efferent terminals and from intrinsic retinal neurons, GABAergic input from intrinsic retinal cells, and direct excitation from GABA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the functional organization of the avian retina and the role of efferent input in the processing of visual information.
the function of the avian efferent projection and the mechanisms by which efferent neurons control the activity of their target cells.
understanding the function of the avian efferent pathway, which is the only known example of an efferent pathway that is not involved in the pupillary light reflex.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the avian TC receives excitatory input from retinal neurons, and this input is mediated by glutamate, GABA, and possibly glycine.
TCs are the only known neurons in the vertebrate retina with both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic input.
TCs are a unique class of amacrine cell with both intrinsic and retinal inputs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the efferent pathway is a mixed excitatory/inhibitory pathway that is capable of both modulating and integrating the activity of the retina.
TCs receive excitatory input from retinal amacrine cells as well as efferent neurons and that TCs are capable of generating APs in response to these inputs.

TCs are a novel type of retinal neuron that receives excitatory glutamatergic and GABAergic inputs, and that their output is a function of both local retinal activity, and descending input from a midbrain center.
The main takeaway from our work is that
TCs are retinal interneurons that receive both retinal input and descending midbrain input, and they integrate this information to generate a retinotopic map in the midbrain.
the TCs are not simply slaves to their midbrains, but rather they reflect local retinal activity as well as midbrain input.
TCs receive a complex mixture of synaptic input from multiple classes of retinal neurons, and this input is excitatory, rather than inhibitory, in nature.
